units.text: ON DEVELOPMENT AND ITS LIMITATIONS 137 ON DEVELOPMENT AND ITS LIMITATIONS

THE subject upon which, by the kind invitation of your Secretary and Committee, I am asked to speak this afternoon to the members of your Union is large and difficult and in some sense still novel. It is a big thing to discuss, even in outline, the sense in which Christianity had the right to develop, and the extent to which, between the first century and the twentieth, it has in fact developed. It is a hard thing to attain to a right equipoise in giving due weight alike to considerations that demand, and considerations that condition, development. And it is more or less a new thing; for not only does the term itself hardly (I suppose) go back beyond the publication of Newman's great work in 1845, but the whole attitude of mind which development embodies in a definitive word depends on, and corresponds to, the growth among us of historical criticism. Even though I shall take the simpler road and start from the observance and examination of the actual facts, I am afraid that, in trying to follow out our thought to just conclusions, this paper may make some inroad upon the attention, the patience, and perhaps even upon the prejudices and presuppositions, of its hearers. Nevertheless, the task seems to be worth attempting.

Nothing, then, in the intellectual sphere distinguishes more clearly the Christianity of the last hundred years from the Christianity of all the centuries that preceded than the emergence and dominance of the historical spirit. For good or for evil, we have learned to look upon our religion historically.

We cannot stand outside the mental orientation and equipment of our own age; and the science of history, as applied to Christianity, was almost newborn in the nineteenth century. Whether we look on the history of the Christian society from within or from without, with sympathy or with criticism, with passionate absorption or with cold disdain, we have all of us to conceive of a process in which each period is linked on to what precedes and what follows, and the elements of continuity and of change in this perpetual process have to be estimated and compared. Development is nothing more nor less than the concentration of this conception into a single term: it is neither a bogy to be frightened of, nor a magical charm and talisman to save us trouble, but the symbol of a new method. To John Henry Newman we owe, if not the word itself, at any rate the introduction of the word into the current coin of our theological * [This paper has been rewritten for publication, but its substance has not been greatly changed.-C. H. T.] IV. 21 10 vocabulary; and Newman himself tells us where he found best exemplified the conception and method of which he fixed the name. "It is melancholy to say it, but the chief, perhaps the only, English writer who has any claim to be considered an ecclesiastical historian is the infidel Gibbon."* If it is in general true to say that no conclusion in the domain of Christian theology is likely to show itself satisfying or valid unless it allows for the coexistence and mutual interaction of diverse and seemingly contradictory elements, then this problem of development, theologically regarded, is only of a piece with the other problems which Christianity calls on us to face. For certainly of this problem nothing can pretend to be an adequate solution which does not find room for the fundamental elements of both stability and progress, or, if you prefer the quasi-scientific terminology of our day, both the static and the dynamic elements. Our New Testament documents themselves express the germ of both ideas. There is the faith once delivered to the saints, the faith of the leaders held up for imitation by their followers, that is, Jesus Christ, the same yesterday, to-day, and for ever; but there is also the office of the Paraclete, who is to lead us into all the truth. We have the truth already, yet we have to be guided into its fulness.t

Our problem, then, is to correlate the one element to the other, to try and see, in broad outline, how and to what degree the fixed element is to condition and control the element of movement. In this inquiry the obvious line for an historian to take is to examine the facts, in, order to see what has been the actual course of events in this or that department of Christian life and doctrine. And I am sanguine enough to think that there is material worth collecting, and that the investigation ought' not to be without result.

One topic beyond all others held and focussed the interest of Christian thinkers of the first generations, as they tried to draw out the implications of the faith they believed and to exercise upon them their faculties of reasoning. "What think ye of Christ~" was the question that pressed insistently for an answer; and the work of Christian theology from St. Paul to St. Athanasius was in the main the effort to provide it.

If the Creed of Nicrea-the confession that Jesus Christ is coeternal and consubstantial with the Father-had been put before any ordinary Greek-speaking Christian of the primitive community at Jerusalem, he would certainly have found it * Development p. 5. [All references are to the original edition. In the editions from 1878 onwards the book is to some extent recast, no doubt to the advantage both of its arrangement and of its style. But it was the book of 1845 not any later reeasti ng of it, which marked an epoeh.] , t Jude 8; Reb. xiii,7,8;John xvi,13. quite unintelligible; it was cast, he would have said, in terms that meant nothing to him. The utmost that one could suggest is that if a Catholic and an Arian formula had both been presented for his acceptance, he would have found more jarring elements in the latter than in the former; and I am not sureremember that we are thinking of the time behind St. Paul's earliest epistles-that it would be true to say even so much. But merely to point the contrast between formulated and unformulated theology does not take us far. It is no solution of the problem. If, on the other hand, we set ourselves patiently to follow out the facts that lie between Jerusalem and Niceea, we shall find that the history of the first three centuries after Christ is the history in this respect of an agelong process, in the course of which Christians were working out slowly, tentatively, painfully, the essential content of the ideas which had formed round the person of their Master from the time of His life among men. As they tried to plumb the secret of the impression that from the first He made on them, and of the attitude in which from the first they found themselves standing towards Him, some forms of explanation were tried which failed in the end to satisfy, experiment was made of some paths which were found to lead to no issue. Yet all along advance was being made, now rapidly, as during the Apostolic age, now more slowly, in times when new thoughts were gradually absorbednow as it were by instinct, now by the more leisurely process of reasoning, most often, perhaps, by the negative method of rejecting solutions that were offered, till the long story culminated in the issue raised by the Arian conception of the nature of the Son of God and the crystallizing of the Catholic refusal of it in the Creed of Nicrea. And still another halfcentury had to pass before the victory of the Catholic cause was assured throughout the Greek and Latin Churches, and the work of Niceea was finally ratified at Constantinople. Development had clearly been at work. Scholars have rightly emphasized, as a speaking testimony to the honesty and accuracy of St. Luke's work, the inchoate and elementary character of the Christian theology embodied in the first chapters of the Acts: the original preaching of the Gospel covered, it would seem, no more than these three points, that Jesus of Nazareth was the Messiah of prophecy, that He had really and truly risen from the dead, and that a message of universal salvation was to go out in His Name. It is a far cry from this to the Homoousion, and it was not to be expected that the course of evolution from the one to the other would run all smooth. Theology has its ups and downs. In the stress of establishing some great advance, too little care perhaps is taken not to overpass the due proportion of truth, and incautious statements of great doctors have seriously embarrassed later generations. Even the early elan of Christian enthusiasm has been convicted by certain modern critics of harbouring "the germs of adoptionism. "God hath made Him both Lord and Christ," cried the Apostle: what wonder, when the point to establish was the present lordship of the Risen and Ascended Jesus 1 That was the one thing in St. Peter's mind: Christian faith must be firmly fixed on that, before it harked back to face the mystery of His pre-existence. Yet we know how confidently St. Paul had taken that next great step when he wrote to the Corinthians and the Philippians: 7TAOVUI,O~tJv €7TTWX€VCT€ (2 Cor. viii. 9), EV~op<PiJ (8)€OV v1TapxCJJv eaVTOV €K€VWCT€V (Phil. ii. 6, 7).* It would be attractive, if time permitted, to describe in detail the stages of the advance through St. John and St. Ignatius, in Irenreus and in Origen, and to note the sudden emergence in each great writer of some new formula, taking up and concentrating the scattered elements of preceding thought, some bold precision that in turn is slowly digested and assimilated till it becomes part and parcel of the common tradition of the whole body. Athanasius is from one point of view a great innovator, but it is on the basis of a continually growing determination of theological thought and language that he gathers up the latent conviction of the Christian body into a challenge embodied in a single word. How unintelligible this process would be without some such conception as that of development to be our guide and clue, we shall best realize if we cast our eyes back for a moment to the aspect which the facts presented when for the first time they began to be matter of familiar treatment and disputed interpretation in the controversies of the seventeenth century.

Almost suddenly, in the stress of the counter-Reformation movement, patristic learning became, more or less about A.D. 1600, an essential weapon in the theological armoury of the day. In turning over the massive tomes into which the scholars of that time poured their erudition so prodigally, one is of course brought up, now and again, against the gaps in their knowledge, where either new material has since come to light or erroneous estimate of old material has been modified by the work of subsequent scholars: but the first and chief impression is of the width of their horizon and of the powerful * And not St. Paul alone. The authors of the Epistle to the Hebrews and the Apocalypse, for instance, stand in one sense at opposite poles to one another; but both teach in the clearest language the pre-existence of Christ. It was common ground to the writers of the second Christian generation.

sweep and scope of their outlook over Christian antiquity. It is not in the way of knowledge that one is most conscious of a subtle difference between the equipment of the men of that day and our own. It is rather that, in the first place, they left the New Testament writings outside the sphere of their real criticism; the New Testament was sacrosanct, a thing apart; if its meaning was contested, it was to lJe elucidated by the patristic tradition. But, in the second place, this tradition, too, tended to be regarded as a single whole. TIle documents were taken en bloc, and, even where they were examined in their chronological order, no sufficient attempt was made to trace the nexus that runs through them and both connects and differentiates them. Thus the Church writings of the ante-Nicene period must be, it was assumed, in general agreement or in general disagreement with the Nicene theology, although either conclusion meant a good deal of straining of the evidence. Only historical criticism, only the conception of development, could provide the master-key: and historical criticism (in the fullest sense) of the Christian origines was still an undiscovered science. Denys Petau-or, to give his name in its latinized form, Dionysius Petavius-was, like Sirmond and Bellarmine, one of the great polymaths of the Jesuit order in its golden age, before the primacy of learning passed to the Benedictines. Petau wrote on many subjects, but we are concerned only with one small section, the preface and first eight chapters of the first book of the second of the five volumes of his vast conspectus of Christian theology, Theoloqicorum Dogmatum. * He was impressed by the difficulty of squaring a good deal of the ante-Nicene theology with the Nicene standard; and if he deserves praise for the honesty with which he faced facts, one is a little tempted to believe that he took some pleasure in exaggerating them -with a view to the more appropriate introduction of a deus ex machina, in the voice of the Church expressed through the Council and the Creed.

On this side of the Channel, Petau's critical methods met with scant sympathy. The appeal to patristic tradition, whether against Rome or Geneva or Zurich, was the essential mark of Anglican theology, as it shaped itself under the hands of our Caroline divines. To men thus minded the tactics of Petau seemed nothing less than the surrender of the whole position: if his interpretation of the facts was correct, the claim of Arians or Socinians to be the real representatives of pre-Nicene Christianity would be beyond dispute. Therefore when George Bull (then a parish priest, afterwards bishop of St. David's) undertook against Unitarianism the" Defence of the Nicene Faith," it seemed to him crucial to re-examine with meticulous care the witness of primitive writers in relation to the Divinity and the Eternity of the Son (" de Filii TfjJ O/LOOVa-Lq}," "de Filii T{jJ a-vva,,8Lcp "), and having done so to claim the whole literature as Catholic. But, as Newman says,* " out of about thirty writers whom he reviews, he has, for one cause or another, to explain nearly twenty."

Neither the conclusion of Petavius nor the conclusion of Bull represented the wholetruth. The method was inadequate, and the concluaions arrived at were inadequate also. "The one party estimate the theology of the early Fathers by the literal force of their separate expressions or phrases, or by the philosophical opinions of the day; the other by the doctrine of the Catholic Church as afterwards authoritatively declared. The one party argues that they need not have meant more than what was afterwards regarded as heresy; the other answers that there is nothing to prevent their meaning more."t A greater name than even Bull or Petavius resumed the task, when John Henry Newman published in 1845 his Essay on the Development of Christian Doctrine.

I make no attempt, I have no qualification, to speak of this epoch-making work over the whole area of its importance: I am concerned with it at this moment only so far as to see what light the study of the principle of development as contained in it may throw on the problem before us. "Developments growing out of the Question of our Lord's Divinity" is the heading of a section (viii., § 1, p. 397) intended to illustrate the fifth of the" tests of fidelity in development," namely, logical sequence. And the first sentence of the section seemsto suggest that the issue raised by Petavius was directly present to Newman's mind. "No one," he writes, "who has looked ever so little into the theological works of the ancient Church but is aware that the language of the ante-Nicene Fathers, on this subject, may be far more easily accommodated to the Arian hypothesis than the language of the post-Nicene." But in truth Newman did little more than enunciate this platitude, and left the matter there. He had at an earlier point (chapter iii., § 4) criticized effectively the methods of Petavius and still more those of Bull, but his own contribution to the subject debated between them is the suggestion of a connexion between the clearing up of Catholic thought against Arianism and the introduction of the cultus sanaorum, Needless to say that even in this curious argumentation the genius of Newman provides matter to attract and fascinate. But he gives us no help towards the application of the principle of development where development concerns the most fundamental of Christian truths. In the forefront of his vision as he wrestled with the theory of development was not the controversy between Arian and Catholic but the controversy between Roman and Anglican. And perhaps historical criticism was still too inchoate, in relation to the New Testament documents, to permit at that date of a full and free review of all the conditions of the case. We have, therefore, to face the problem for ourselves. 'Ve take our start with the most elementary data offered us in our documents-the Christology, that is, of the earliest chapters of the Book of Acts-and then try to realize the sort of process that went on during the three centuries which intervened between Pentecost and the Council of Niceea, as Christians were consciously and unconsciously working out, whether under the leading of their religious experience or by more purely intellectual processes, the implications of their original ideas and feelings and convictions about their Master and Lord. That is what we mean by development, as a necessary postulate for the explanation of the history of Christian thought. In the light of this conception the difficulties felt by seventeenthcentury scholars about primitive Christologies vanish away: for it is only what we should expect if we find that, at each stage of the effort to draw out the essential content of the inherited tradition and express it in a rational synthesis, many forms of statement were hazarded and found wanting and were replaced by others more satisfactory, until a relatively final term was achieved in the formulary of Niceea.

Indeed, it is perhaps most often when defective theologies work themselves out to full and explicit completeness in forms which are felt to be irreconcilable with the Christian religion, that a definite step is taken forward: in this sense error is normally a condition precedent of the exacter comprehension of truth. The later growths at least of the Creed were due not so much to any positive liking for definitions of faith as to the need of some plain statement that such and such an interpretation of the fundamental Christian data, recommended as the last word in theology, was, on the contrary, either disastrously one-sided or actually false. Without Arius there would have been no Nicene Creed. It does not, of course, follow that a continued repetition of the process " new errors, more stringent definitions," is at all to be desired.

But, true as it is that development not only did take place but took place rightly, is it the whole truth 1 Is there not a danger that the glamour of one great and illuminating conception may blind us to another aspect of truth worth our while to consider 1 Granted that, as things were, and as perhaps they must have been, the process of creed-formation was necessary and inevitable; allowing to the full that by this road the common Christian consciousness had arrived at conclusions and worked out results which could never be called into question again; recognizing gladly that to the attainment of this end was devoted some of the highest effort, of mind and soul alike, of which humanity has shown itself capable: even so, there is something to be set on the other side. Of all definitions, that of Niceea brought the greatest gain to Christian theology at the smallest price. Yet perhaps no general rule is of more universal application than this, that every great advance is attended with some corresponding loss, however relatively slight the loss may be.

In the first place there is in the earlier writers an atmosphere of freedom and vigour which, as definition progresses, begins to make itself less and less felt. Definition means a limit put to the unrestricted play and movement of Christian thought. One-sided, or if you like erroneous, phraseology, to be found here and there in Ignatius and Ireneeus, in Tertullian and Origen, is the inevitable drawback to the swift and daring flight of the finest intellects of the first Christian generations as they directed their vision to the great mysteries of religion. The air is something less exhilarating even in the fourth century than it had been in the second and third: it becomes heavier, at moments oppressive, as the centuries go on.

But, secondly, the loss which development may involve is to be traced in more direct ways than the mere circumscription of Christian thought. Man prizes most what he has won at greatest cost: and so, the fiercer the contest over the establishmend of any dogma of our Creed, the more exclusive a position will that doctrine hold when the struggle is over and the security of its place among the Christian credenda is at last assured. Where it has been found necessary to define a truth, to commend it in a permanent formula to the safe keeping of the Christian people, it will nearly always happen that the truth so commended obtains a pre-eminence which is liable, in spite of all the care of theologians, to disturb the delicate balance of Catholic faith. Development, that is to say, has its special element of danger: we need to be always on our guard against its over-reaching itself.

I know that it may seem a paradox to suggest that the victory of the cause for which Athanasius fought and suffered brought with it anything less than clear gain. The very existence of Christianity in any full sense of the term was at stake over the Homoousion. Athanasius was no irresponsible bigot, but -a theologian with a marked sense of restraint and an unusual capacity for seeing below the surface of things. Never-theless, even so, the teaching of the Alexandrine and the Western Churches did receive from that time onwards an accentuated bias in one direction; a difference can be traced, in those Churches, between ante-Nicene and post-Nicene theology which is not wholly to the advantage of the latter. Exactly where Newman finds, for the purpose he had in view, the advantages of development-since the cultus of the saints and the Blessed Virgin can, on his showing, be deduced from the new tendency that emerges in the West after the Council of Nicooa-exactly there it may be that development needs to be tested at every turn by the standard of earlier ages and the tradition of the Church. Nor am I thinking here merely of the over-subtle line of argument by which Newman seeks to " develop" the cultus of the saints out of the Nicene theology: other things were affected in the direction of fundamental Christian thought and worship.

I do not suppose that a Catholic Christian of the fourth century would have been conscious of any change in his religion as the outcome of the Nicene faith and creed. The confession of belief expressed in the Homoousion was, ill his conviction as in ours, the only possible issue of the original premisses of Christian teaching; and the whole doctrinal tradition was so strong and vigorous that there was no danger of any immediate supersession of other and complementary truths. And in the Eastern Churches the influence of the great Cappadocian Fathers, Basil and the two Gregories, to say nothing of the school of Antioch, was a sufficient makeweight against onesided tendencies. But, at least as to certain departments of biblical exegesis, the temptation was strong in Alexandrine and Western circles to abandon earlier interpretations wherever encouragement seemed to be afforded by them to the Arian propaganda.

Thus the text" My Father is greater than I " (John. xiv. 28) was by early writers quite regularly explained of the preeminence of the Eternal Father as Father in relation to the Eternal Son as Son: and the traditional exegesis is repeated in the fourth century by Alexander and Athanasius at Alexandria and by Hilary and Marius Victorinus in the West, as well as by Basil and Gregory in the East. But in view of the emphasis with which the Arian party pressed their deductions from the text so explained, it came to seem the simpler course to cut the ground from under them by limiting its application to our Lord's humanity; and this became, I think, the constant usage of the Latin Church. Nevertheless it has against it the practically unanimous consent not only of the ante-Nicene Fathers but of the Nicene generation as well.

Or, again, the appearances to the patriarchs and others of a supernatural visitant from God, recorded in the Old Testament, had been always interpreted by primitive Christian writers, as well as by the Council which condemned Paul of Samosata at Antioch, as being in a true sense Theophanies, anticipations in some mysterious way of the supreme Theophany of the Incarnation; and it was easy for Arians to suggest that there must be a difference of nature between the Father, whom no man hath seen at any time, and th.e Son, who could thus render Himself visible. Once more the Latin Fathers, never quite at home with the subtle distinctions in which the genius of Greek theology found its metier, conceived it more compatible with the defenceof the Homoousion to strike out a new line and interpret the " Angel " of a created being rather than of the Eternal Son. Through the influence of St. Augustine this view came to prevail so exclusively in the West that Newman can speak of it as " the explicit doctrine which has been received since his date."* But, as Dr. Liddon admits,'] "the earlier interpretation has been more generally advocated by English divines "; and one of ·the most learned of the second generation of Tractarian theologians has defended it at great length and with the support of a vast catena of patristic citations.j These were, in themselves, unimportant consequences: they did not touch the faith or life of the ordinary man. But they were symptomatic of others, less obvious and less immediate, which go deeper and approach the foundations of the Christian religion. So slow, indeed, were these latter of growth that they are hardly traceable before medieeval times and perhaps did not seriously disturb the balance of truth before the Reformation. But much post-Reformation theology, both Catholic and Protestant, has in different ways been affected by them.

Among the questions that could not fail sooner or later to demand insistently an answer, as the Christian Church tried to work out the premisses of its belief to their full conclusions, had been this-whether prayer was properly to be addressed to Christ. Now in a pagan world monotheism was the base and startingpoint of Christianity in a much more real sense than it is nowadays. And I suppose that a Christian of the apostolic generation, if asked to whom he addressed his prayers, would have replied that he prayed to his God and Father through Jesus Christ his Lord. Through Christ the high priest access is obtained to God, in Christ the Beloved acceptance is found before the Father. And this primitive instinct is enshrined for us to all time in the traditional language of the Church's common worship. Scholars have been beginning of late years * Development, viii., § 1, p. 398.

to realize how archaic an element of Christian life is represented for us in the liturgy of the Eucharist. Here Christian prayer was translated into corporate action; and the address of Eucharistic prayer was to God the Father alone. Anything else would have been a contradiction of all that antiquity stood for. Did then this constant tradition of common worship, expressed in the liturgies of East and West and continued in post-Nicene times in the series of Roman collects, so many of which survive in our own Prayer-Book, exclude from the purview of Christian religious life the direct address of prayer to Jesus Christ 1

No: for, constant and venerable as is the tradition which restricted the direction of Eucharistic prayer, another tradition, hardly less ancient or less clearly defined, has come down side by side with it-that of the hymnody of the Church and its address to Christ. The earliest reference in a non-Christian source to meetings for Christian worship is contained in the letter of Pliny the younger, when Governor of Bithynia (A.D.112), to the Emperor Trajan, and the central point of the account is the singing of a hymn to Christ. * About a century later a writer, probably to be identified with Hippolytus, appealed, as to a custom whereof the memory of man ran not to the contrary, to the "theologizing" of "the Word of God, the Christ," in Christian psalms and songs.] The most ancient of such compositions that have come down to us are doubtless the two Greek morning and evening hymns, a6ga EV Vl/J£CTTOL( the Gloria in excelsis) and <Pw~LAapov: of the latter the authorship was already forgotten ill St. Basil's time, but he attributes it to " the fathers,"] while the former is among the numerous documents recast to form the Apostolic Oonstitutions, § and no one of the documents so recast is later than the third century.
* "Carmen Christo quasi deo dicere secum inuicem" (Ep. Plinii ad Traianum).

My colleague, Dr. Brightman, reminds me that, as " carmen dicere" had a more or less technical meaning in pagan ritual, Pliny's language may imply that the Christian congregation was repeating a form of words after the officiant. as forms of prayer which the minister-presumably the deacon-said first and the people repeated " in common " after him. Here then we should see the beginnings of the litanies of intercession, addressed to our Lord, which we find regularly in the liturgies. In both our Lord is directly addressed; and both may well have been included among the " psalms to our Lord Jesus Christ" which 'Paul of Samosata suppressed at Antioch as novel inventions. * Whether or no Paul was right about the age of the particular hymns he had in mind, he was quite wrong, as the evidence' just cited demonstrates, in asserting the novelty of the practice: the hymns may have been modern, the tradition of hymning Christ was ancient. And the hymnody of later days has certainly tended to concentrate itself more and more on this type to the exclusion of all others. The Preface to the last edition of Hymns Ancient and Modern, admitting that " it is often urged as an objection to Christian hymn-books, that so great a proportion of the hymns contained in them are addressed to our Blessed Redeemer rather than to the Father to whom He brings us," throws the responsibility rather on the composers of our hymns than on the compilers of the collections. Following then the historical method, we have established the coexistence in the early Church of two sets of data, between which there is some prima facie inconsistency-the stringent limitation of Eucharistic prayer and the wider address of hymnody. How are we to reconcile them 1 Are we to say that development leads us away from the one to the other, and that it is a legitimate deduction from the faith of Niceea that even Eucharistic prayer may rightfully be addressed to our Lord 1 Or should we not rather say that the peril of development is just that it tends to make us forget that a concentration of emphasis on one article of the Creed may, if unchecked and unconditioned, disturb that proportion of truth which is the preservative of sane religion 1

We shall find a truer approach to a satisfactory synthesis if, instead of undervaluing either of the two elements of primitive tradition, we ask for what each of them stood, and why hymnody should have formed as it were an exception to a general rule of Christian worship.

The creed of the Christian began, and must always begin, with the confession of one God the Father Almighty; and so the first recorded instance of Christian common prayer is addressed to the Lord of all,~v SEO"7Tora (Acts iv, 24). But equally the first recorded instance of ejaculatory prayer of a Christian martyr at the crisis of his agony is addressed to the Saviour, KVPL€ 'I1]O"ov, SEgaL TO 7TV€V/La /LOV (Acts vii. 59). And the long centuries of Christian experience have generation by generation ratified the appeal, and in their moments of anguish and desolation Christian hearts have turned to Him who knows the trials Thus in Christian worship hymns or litanies addressed to our Redeemer are the natural and proper satisfaction of the Christian instinct of loyalty to Christ. They represent the emotional element, and the emotions have their right place, though a subordinate place, in worship. Even in the Eucharist we may intercalate the adoring cry Agnus Dei, qui tollis peccata mundi, miserere nobis. But especially in the Eucharist shall we do well to guard jealously the principle of the Church's tradition of worship. There the priestly people, through and with their High Priest, plead the One Sacrifice before God. The early liturgies left no opening for the dangers to which some more modern phases of Christianity might expose us. There is no room for any contrast between a righteous Father and His merciful Son, any more than between a righteous Son and His merciful mother. The prayers in them are the prayers of Christians who, while they believed as firmly as we do in the Presence of Christ in the Sacrament, did not forget that the Gift given us is the Father's Gift, and the service offered throughout the rite is a single service from the beginning to the end. To lose the sense of the solemn restraint with which the ancient Church guarded its monotheism by tuning its common Eucharistic worship and self-dedication to the note of response to the Father's love would be not only to break all real liturgical continuity: it would be to endanger, under the shelter of development, a true safeguard of theological balance. Developments, even the greatest and most important of them all, need to be tested by repeated reference to primitive standards.

Of course, it is not easy to distinguish between legitimate development and its less legitimate consequences. But theology, divinarum rerum scientia, was never meant to be an easy thing. We are on safest ground when we remember that Christian theology should be at every step a harmonization of different aspects of truth. Now if development needs guarding even when it starts from clear implications of the New Testament, and leads to the full definition of so fundamental an article of our faith as the Divinity of our Lord-if even the Nicene confession can be so emphasized to the neglect of other elements of our religion as to affect the equipoise of theological thought-if even here it is an advantage to correct our compasses from time to time by reference to the Scriptures and tradition of the earliest generations of the Church-it is not likely that the case will be otherwise on any lesser issues. Developments are inevitable: we cannot expect to do without them, and should often be the worse if we tried to do without them; but we need in dealing with them some more effective instrument of control than the tests which Newman prescribes, and we shall only find what we need in constant recurrence to the apostolic Scriptures and the apostolic tradition.
Let me take two illustrations from developments, actual or proposed, in matters less vital but yet not negligible.
1. The first illustration shall be from the history of the Sacrament that we call Confirmation.

How large a part development has here played, during the nineteen Christian centuries, we shall realize if we contrast Confirmation with Baptism. There have been changes even in the administration of Baptism, and controversies even over the external aspects of it. But for all that, not only is it still retained by almost all bodies calling themselves Christian, but there is an obvious identity in the rite as practised to-day and as practised in the age of the Apostles. It would be impossible to say as much of Confirmation, whether we regard the differences of usage between one Christian body and another-to say nothing of the sects that have abandoned it altogether-or the differences between each and the Church of the Apostles.

For one thing, Confirmation was in early days, from the New Testament onwards, not a separate sacrament to itself; but essentially one thing with the Sacrament of Baptism: it is by exception if they are called two sacraments. What in the New Testament is called Baptism with the Spirit is, as I understand it, nothing else than the Gift of the Spirit imparted through the laying on of hands that accompanied Baptism: and in the only ancient treatise that touches specifically on the distinction between the two rites they are correlated as " baptisma aqure " and "baptisma spiritus." But differentiation between them has gone on increasing until Baptism and Confirmation are regarded, and have for many centuries been regarded, as two sacraments, separated normally in the West, in the Roman Church and in our own, by a considerable period of years. It has, of course, to be remembered that when most baptisms were those of adult converts, and were administered in the presence of, if not by, the bishop, the connexion of the two rites was dictated by the circumstances, and the circumstances changed when most baptisms came to be those of infants, and, since the bishop could not be ubiquitous, were administered by the local clergy.

Further, in the Roman Church communion is habitually given, as it never was in the primitive Church, before Confirmation, But developments have affected not only the intimate association of Confirmation with Baptism, but also both the " matter" (to use a technical word) and the ministrant of the sacrament itself.

In the New Testament, Confirmation is described in terms of the laying on of hands, and" laying on of hands" remained the definition of the rite throughout primitive times in the Western Church. But anointing, or "chrism," was from remote, perhaps even from apostolic, * days a supplementary part of the rite; and what was at first only a supplement became in the Eastern Church, as early as the third or fourth century, the essential and even the only" matter" of the sacrament. In time, too, though very much later, the Roman Churchfollowed suit on the same lines, so that the apostolic" matter" of Confirmation survives only among ourselves and some Lutheran bodies; while on the other hand we have to our loss dropped the significant and it may be original accompaniment of the unction.

Lastly, the minister of Confirmation was in the New Testament the Apostle, and in early post-apostolic generations the bishop. But the Greek Church, when the laying on of hands fell out, transferred also the ministration of the rite from bishops to presbyters, though the bishop's authority over the sacrament has been so far retained that the chrism is always consecrated by the bishop. The Western Church has in practice reserved the administration of Confirmation to the bishop, though Gregory the Great allowed presbyters by delegation to confirm in Sardinia, and in general the Roman theory is that presbyters can (though I presume only by Papal authority) be commissioned to confirm.] But in the primitive view the laying on of hands over the Christian people in Confirmation Was as naturally reserved to the Apostle or bishop as the laying on of hands over Christian ministers in Ordination: the Gift of the Spirit was one and the same, notwithstanding the diversities of xapLCTjLaTa in its purpose and application. It can be no small cause for gratitude that this apostolic tradition, which alone gives full meaning and dignity to the Sacrament of Confirmation, survives among ourselves.

Certainly, even where the rite and the ministrant have been altered, no one would wish to deny the reality of the sacrament. Because the intention to perform the apostolic rite has been present all along, and because the development has been spread over a large area of Christian Churches and over long generations of Christian life, we cannot disallow the things done, however much we may regret them. 2. My second illustration I take from the burning topic of the ministry of women.

From the first Christianity proclaimed the complete spiritual equality of men and women, their identical right to enter by baptism into membership of the Christian Society, their one participation in the gift of the Spirit and the fellowship of the Eucharist, their common title to citizenship here and hereafter in the Kingdom of Christ. But more than this: in the intercessions of the Widows on the 'Church's roll, in the self-dedication of the Virgins to the unmarried state, in the active ministration of the Deaconesses,provision was made for special types of the religious life and work of women.

This was much; and it went far beyond anything that paganism or even Judaism had conceived. Yet on the other hand, from the time of our Lord and the Apostles onward,there was a clear distinction drawn, and the ministry open to women was the ministry of service and not the ministry of office, the serving of the needs of the members of Christ and not the preaching of the Gospel. Women were among our Lord's nearest and closest followers, they ministered to Him of their substance and doubtless cared for His bodily wants, but He did not send them out among the Seventy or choose them among the Apostles.

The middle path of the Christian Church in this matter remained in marked contrast alike to the inequalities fostered by paganism on the one side, and to the licence allowed by pseudo-Christians on the other. Marcus Aurelius the Emperor is for us the finished type of ascetic goodness on the basis of philosophy: and Marcus looks out on life in the capacity of " a male and a Roman,"* whereas in Christ we know that there is neither Roman nor barbarian, neither male nor female. Conversely, heretical sects, and some that were not strictly heretical, permitted and encouraged a ministry of women: Montanists had official prophetesses, Marcionites had female ministers, and it is suggested that in this they were but developing on their own account the principles of Christian liberty. Even if they were before their time, may they not (it is asked) rank as examples of that fourth test of Newman's which he calls" early anticipation," and have prematurely foreshadowed a" movement which is now rightly coming to its own 1 * Meditation8 ii, 5, W!; 'PWj.laLO!; leaL appqv. Any such interpretation of the facts, however seductive at first sight, falls to the ground when we recognize the filiation of Montanist prophecy from Phrygian paganism, and remember the energizing in Gnostic thought of a principle fundamentally antagonistic to Christianity. All Gnostics, in whatever else they differed, agreed in regarding the material world around us as essentially evil. Christianity was a religion compatible with the ordered progress of human society, Marcionism was an anti-social religion in its rejection of marriage. Religions of this latter type encourage the emergence of woman in the public sphere, just because they sweep away her true preeminence in family life-whether, like the Montanists, they only exaggerate the ascetic element, or, like the Marcionites, exalt it into the dominant principle of their theology.

There is then a strong presumption against accepting any development which runs counter to the constant tradition and interpretation of the Church. On the other hand, development, however carefully it needs to be watched and guarded, cannot be ruled out (we have seen) as such; still less can we draw any dividing-line and say that development was legitimate down to a certain date, but is not legitimate now. The work of the Spirit in the Body was not brought to an end when the Creed was formulated, nor even when the external unity of the Church was shattered. No doubt it is not so simple on our Anglican theory as it is on the Roman to find easy room for development, and indeed it may be just as well that it is not. But it has been a weakness of the Anglican position, both as against Rome and as against modernism, that it has sometimes seemed to fix a rigid limit of time and to treat the Church down to that particular moment as a living organism, creating and developing the equipment appropriate for its life, but after that moment as a perfectly equipped machine which has nothing more to do than to travel on indefinitely in the grooves to which it has been fitted. The life of the Spirit-bearing Body cannot be so confined. We may, indeed, believe that what has once been forged with blood and tears, like the faith of Nicsea, is KTi}JLa E~aEL, an acquired possession of which nothing can rob us. But somewhere in our theology we must find room for the possibility of development; and we cannot be sure that development, in the generations to come, may not lead us in unexpected directions. Sixty or seventy years ago no one would have guessed how far a silent revolution in our doctrine of final things would affect us. Yet this has not been among ourselves alone, nor does it lead entirely away from the tradition of the early Church. Still wider in its working throughout Western Europe is the movement that threatens to reverse the oldest IV. 21 11 and greatest of all developments which Christianity has experienced in its contact with the world. Sixteen centuries have passed since Constantine and the ecclesiastics of his court inaugurated their fatal alliance between Church and State. Will the elder among us live to witness the reversal of a policy so far-reaching and of such long standing, and see realized in England the vision of Libera Chiesa in Libero Stato? Dies docebit about that and other things. But there are, I am sure, enough changes which would bring things into nearer accord with the ideals of the Prophet of Nazareth and His first followers to satisfy the impulses of the most revolutionary among us. Developments may be for the better or for the worse; and if they seem to lead us away from the example of Christ and the teaching of His Church in the days when its inspiration was still fresh, we may at least claim that they must be first submitted to a searching test of time.
C. H. TURNER.
THE GROUP MIND OF THE CHURCH

THE study of Social Science has resulted in the discovery of the " Group Mind." A crowd, an army, a nation, is not a mere collection of separate individuals. It has an individuality, a quasi-personality of its own, embracing all the individuals of which it is composed, drawing from them their personal characteristics, and combining them in a unity which is greater than the mere sum of them. The crowd will do things which the individuals composing it blush to remember; the army performs deeds of heroism of which the soldier would be incapable, apart from his comrades. And as to a nation, Dr. McDougall, in his study of the" Group Mind," maintains that" a society when it enjoys a long life, and becomes highly organized, acquires a structure and qualities which are largely independent of the qualities of the individuals who enter into its composition and take part for a brief while in its life. It becomes an organized system of forces which has a life of its own, a power of moulding all its component individuals, and a power of perpetuating itself as a self-identical system, subject only to slow and gradual change." . In this gradual change of the society dominated by the Group Mind we trace progress or deterioration, as the case may be. The movement of social life runs along two distinct lines, moral and intellectual, and is conditioned in both by the innate and acquired characteristics of the race.
